cards.explanation: The answer is speak wickedness, friends. Job says, "…my lips will not speak wickedness, and my tongue will not utter deceit." (Job 27:4) He ties it to his breath, so the promise runs as long as he's breathing. That's a promise with no expiration date, and I can't even keep a timer promise on a batch.

The answer is False, friends. Job says, "I will never say that you are right; I will maintain my integrity until I die." (Job 27:5) No giving in, no "okay, you win." This man has dug in like dough in a cold bowl.

The answer is his conscience. Job says, "As long as I live, my conscience will not accuse me." (Job 27:6) He's saying his own inner voice has nothing to charge him with. That's a big claim, and I think he means every word.

The answer is, will God hear his cry, friends. Job asks, "Will God hear his cry when distress comes upon him?" (Job 27:9) It's a question, and Job leaves it hanging for his friends to chew on. He follows it with more questions about the godless man in the next verse.

The answer is True, friends. Job asks, "Will he delight in the Almighty? Will he call upon God at all times?" (Job 27:10) It's the same string of questions about the godless man, one after another. Job keeps asking about him in these verses.

The word is empty, friends. Job says, "Why then do you keep up this empty talk?" (Job 27:12) He's telling his friends they've seen it for themselves, so why all the hot air? I've heard some empty talk in my day, mostly from a coupon in a drawer that still believed in itself.

The answer is False, friends. Job says, "Though his sons are many, they are destined for the sword; and his offspring will never have enough food." (Job 27:14) Lots of sons, but destined for the sword, not long and peaceful lives. A heavy verse, so I'll just let it sit.

The answer is that they will not weep for them, friends. Job says, "…and their widows will not weep for them." (Job 27:15) It's a heavy line, and I think it's meant to sound that heavy. I'll just let it sit.

The answer is True, friends. Job says, "…what he lays up, the righteous will wear, and his silver will be divided by the innocent." (Job 27:17) All that piling up, and somebody else ends up wearing it. That's one expensive way to dress someone else.

The answer is a hut set up by a watchman, friends. Job says the house is "…like a moth’s cocoon, like a hut set up by a watchman." (Job 27:18) Neither one is built to last. Two pictures, same message: flimsy.

The word is wealthy, friends. Job says, "He lies down wealthy, but will do so no more; when he opens his eyes, all is gone." (Job 27:19) He goes to sleep with everything and wakes up with nothing. I'd be checking under the pillow.

The answer is without mercy, friends. Job says, "It hurls itself against him without mercy as he flees headlong from its power." (Job 27:22) He's running flat out, and the wind keeps coming. No softening it.

The answer is False, friends. Job says, "It claps its hands at him and hisses him out of his place." (Job 27:23) The wind is sending him away, not welcoming him back home. That's about as warm as a cold oven.
